head:
Strength · Women

Women and strength: putting an end to received ideas

Women are weaker than men, they progress less, they risk gaining size they never wanted. These three sentences circulate in gyms as if they belonged together. The studies read for this article say the first is true on average and the other two do not hold, or not the way people think. We follow a single question, from the broadest to the most precise, down to what remains uncertain.

The problem

In a strength test, a woman often sees a lower number than a man of the same age. In many gyms, this observation has become a rule: “women are not made for strength”, “their gains are slower”, “they should avoid heavy loads”. When a norm table separates levels by sex, some read it as confirmation of this idea. Others see the opposite, a norm table that behaves as if the gap did not exist.

Both readings share the same difficulty. A difference in averages between two groups is a statistical fact. It does not say what a given person can do, where the gap comes from, or what happens when people train. To answer, several things need to be separated: the size of the gap, its cause, how each sex responds to training, and what comes from perceptions and habits rather than from the body.

The question

What strength gap really exists between men and women, where does it come from, and what does it change, in practice, for a woman who wants to do strength training?

We proceed in six steps. First the size of the gap. Then its cause. Then the response to training, the question of “unwanted size gain” and the variability between people. After that come the special cases (over 50, trained athletes, fatigue), then the objections and what remains uncertain. The answer follows, with what you can put in place.

What is at stake

What is at stake is not theoretical. First, there is the choice of whether to train or not. If you believe your progress will be slower or that heavy loads will make you “bulky”, you may stay away from it, or train too light for anything to happen. A false idea that keeps you away from a type of training costs time and results.

Then there is how you read your own level. A test number only means something when compared with a reference. Comparing your result with a man’s, or with a norm table that ignores the averages of your group, can make you miss your real progress. Conversely, thinking that every gap is biological can make you give up work that is effective.

There is muscle mass over time. In an imaging study of 468 adults aged 18 to 88, the share of muscle in body weight starts to fall from the third decade, and absolute muscle mass only clearly declines towards the end of the fifth decade of life (around age 50), mainly in the legs.2 Muscle is a reserve that wears down with age: the more you have set aside, the more you keep. Since women start on average with less muscle mass than men (it is measured as lower), this reserve matters at least as much for them. This is reasoning, not a study result.

Finally, there is confidence. What you believe is possible determines what you try. This article does not measure that feeling. It checks what the data allow us to say, so that the choice to train rests on facts.
rest:
Step 1 of 6 · The finding

The strength gap exists on average, and it is larger for the upper body

We start with the fact that nobody disputes. In a classic study, 8 men and 8 women were compared on the strength and muscle of the arm (biceps) and thigh. Women developed about 52% of men’s strength for the upper body and about 66% for the lower body.1 The same work measured the cross-sectional area of the muscles: it was smaller in women by 45% for the biceps, 41% for all the elbow flexors, 30% for the vastus lateralis of the thigh and 25% for all the knee extensors.1

Women develop on average half to two thirds of men’s strength, and their muscles are smaller in the same proportion

Women’s values as a percentage of men’s (100 = men). Strength: 52% and 66% as published. Muscle area: 100 minus the published gaps for all the elbow flexors (41%) and knee extensors (25%), so derived. 8 men and 8 women. Source: Miller et al., 1993.1

What this means

For the upper body, the women in this small study have about half of men’s strength. For the lower body, two thirds. If you compare yourself with a man without taking this into account, you are measuring yourself against a group whose average is clearly higher than your group’s. It says nothing about you: it is an average over 16 people.

Figures of the same order appear in a 2026 review that reports the synthesis by Nuzzo (2023): women’s maximal load on the chest press would be 40 to 55% of men’s, and 60 to 65% for the leg press and the squat. These values come second-hand, so they should be taken as an order of magnitude.10 The gap is therefore larger in the upper body than in the lower body, repeatedly.

The logical next step is to find out where this gap comes from. If women’s muscle is less efficient, that is one thing. If there is simply less of it, that is another.

Step 2 of 6 · The cause

The gap mostly follows the amount of muscle, not its quality

In the same study, the ratio between strength and muscle area did not differ significantly between the sexes, either at the elbow or at the knee. The number of biceps fibres did not differ significantly either (about 180,600 in men, 156,900 in women). It was the fibres that were larger in men: on average 6,632 versus 3,963 µm² in the biceps.1 The authors conclude that men’s greater strength comes mainly from larger fibres, and attribute the more marked upper-body gap to a lower proportion of lean tissue in women in that region.

To know whether this holds in a real population, we look at the muscle mass itself. A magnetic resonance imaging study of 468 men and women aged 18 to 88 gives 33.0 kg of skeletal muscle on average in men and 21.0 kg in women. Relative to body weight, that is 38.4% versus 30.6%. The gap is larger for the upper body (about 40%) than for the lower body (about 33%).2

Women have less muscle, especially in the upper body, which reproduces the profile of the strength gap

Women’s values as a percentage of men’s. The percentages are derived from the published averages: 21.0 out of 33.0 for total mass, 30.6 out of 38.4 for the share of body weight; 100 minus 40 and 100 minus 33 for the regions, described as “about” in the source. 468 adults. Source: Janssen et al., 2000 (article record).2

What this means

In both studies, the strength gap and the muscle gap have the same profile: larger for the upper body than for the lower body. This is not proof that everything is explained by mass (the samples differ), but the simplest lead is that a muscle’s strength depends first on its size. In other words: for equal muscle area, strength is comparable. The useful question becomes “how much muscle can I gain?”, not “is my muscle of poor quality?”.

A 2026 review also reports a result in athletes who had been training for at least three years: after adjusting for lean mass, the gaps between men and women in squat, deadlift and vertical jump disappeared for the lower body. Men remained stronger in the bench press and the bench throw.10 Again, second-hand. The message is nuanced: for the lower body, the gap is explained by lean mass; for the upper body, part of it remains unexplained by these studies.

If the gap is mostly a matter of the amount of muscle, the next question is about change: do women gain as much of it as men when they train?

Step 3 of 6 · The response to training

With training, men and women progress in comparable proportions

One of the largest studies is the one by Hubal and colleagues (2005). It had 243 men and 342 women aged 18 to 40 follow 12 weeks of progressive strength training of the elbow flexors, the same for everyone. Result for maximal one-repetition strength: men improve by 39.8% on average, women by 64.1%. In absolute terms, men gain slightly more kilos (4.3 versus 3.6 kg), but women’s relative improvement is significantly greater. For biceps area, men gain 20.4% and women 17.9%, a significant but small difference.5

In twelve weeks, women improve more in relative strength and barely less in muscle size

Mean relative gains after 12 weeks of training of the non-dominant arm. 243 men, 342 women, aged 18 to 40. Source: Hubal et al., Medicine and Science in Sports and Exercise, 2005 (copy of the text).5

What this means

A woman who does strength training does not progress more slowly than men, in proportion to her starting point. A percentage gain compares each person with themselves, which is the right way to read your own progress. One possible reason for women’s larger relative progress: they start lower. This is a hypothesis. The data read do not test it.

A single study, on a single muscle, is not enough. Roberts and colleagues (2020) pooled the studies in which men and women followed the same protocol: 10 studies for muscle gain, 17 for upper-body strength, 23 for lower-body strength. Participants were mostly untrained adults aged 18 to 50.3,4

Gains in muscle and lower-body strength do not differ by sex, and the upper body leans in favour of women

Difference in relative gain between women and men, as an effect size (dot) and 95% confidence interval (line). If the interval contains 0, the difference is not demonstrated. Source: Roberts, Nuckols and Krieger, 2020, meta-analysis.3,4

What this means

For muscle (0.07) and leg strength (−0.21), the line crosses the zero line: no demonstrated difference between the sexes. For the upper body, the whole line is on the women’s side (−0.60, interval from −0.93 to −0.26): they gain more in proportion. Results vary a lot from one study to another for strength (heterogeneity of 72% and 75%), which calls for caution about the exact figure.3,4 In short: nothing justifies expecting slower progress for a woman.

A broader 2025 meta-analysis (29 studies) reaches the same conclusion on muscle: in relative gain, the difference is 0.69% (interval from −1.50 to 2.88%), so indistinguishable from zero.6 The point that remains is the one that worries people most: absolute gains.

Step 4 of 6 · Size and variability

“Unwanted size gain” does not appear in the data, and individual responses vary far more than averages

The same 2025 meta-analysis finds, in absolute terms, a small but certain male advantage (effect size of 0.19, 100% probability of favouring men).6 A report on this study gives a larger gap for the upper body (0.30) than for the lower body (0.17).7 In Hubal’s study, this is what biceps area shows: +4.2 cm² on average in men, +2.4 cm² in women.5

After twelve weeks of biceps training, women’s mean gain is 2.4 cm², and the highest observed is 7.2 cm²

Gain in cross-sectional area of the trained arm’s biceps, in absolute terms. 243 men, 342 women. Source: Hubal et al., 2005 (copy of the text).5

What this means

A progressive strength programme followed for three months gives women on average 2.4 cm² more on the biceps cross-section. This is a real, measurable effect, not a transformation. These studies test a deliberate effort, not an accident: none of the studies read measured an “unwanted” gain in size. What the figures allow us to say is that even when people train to progress, the average gain remains modest over 12 weeks. The percentages are close to men’s, which means a gain proportionate to what you already have.

Then there is variability. In Hubal’s study, individual gains in biceps area ranged from 2 to 59% and those in maximal strength from 0 to 250%. In men, area gained from 2.5 to 55.5%; in women, from 2.3 to 59.3%. For strength: from 0 to 150% in men, from 0 to 250% in women.5

The range of individual responses is almost the same for both sexes, and it is huge

Individual relative gains after 12 weeks, from lowest to highest, with each group’s mean. 243 men and 342 women. Source: Hubal et al., 2005 (copy of the text).5

What this means

Two people of the same sex, on the same programme, can progress by 2% or by 59%. This is the biggest lesson from these data: the average for one sex does not tell you where you will land. Some women gain a lot of muscle, others little, just like men. There is no reason to assume in advance which side you will be on. You find out by training, test after test.

So far, the groups were young and untrained. Do the results hold when the population changes?

Step 5 of 6 · The special cases

After 50, in athletes and in fatigue, the picture becomes clearer without being overturned

After 50

A systematic review with meta-analysis pooled 30 studies, 1,410 people over 50 (651 men, 759 women) who followed the same programme. In relative gain, women progressed more in lower-body strength (g = −0.21, interval from −0.33 to −0.10). For upper-body strength (g = −0.29, interval from −0.62 to 0.04) and muscle size (g = 0.10, interval from −0.04 to 0.23), no difference is demonstrated. In absolute terms, men gain more: upper-body strength (g = 0.48), lower-body (0.33) and muscle size (0.45).8 Another meta-analysis, on 35 studies and 1,142 people aged 60 and over, finds the same thing: differences in absolute terms, not in relative terms. It also finds no difference for chair rises or walking capacity.9 The authors of the first conclude that whether a difference exists depends on how it is measured, in absolute or relative terms.

The practical consequence: at 55 or 65, strength training works in women as it does in men, and function (getting up, walking) improves in the same way.

In trained athletes

The 2026 review reports that, in strength athletes, the ratio of the load lifted to body weight is about 1.5 in men versus 1.0 in women for the bench press, and 2.1 versus 1.6 for the squat. These values come second-hand.10 They show that the gap remains present in highly trained people, and that, relative to body weight, it remains smaller for the legs than for the upper body. They do not say that a woman cannot reach a high level.

Fatigue and recovery

According to the same review, which relies on Hunter (2014), women are generally more resistant to fatigue in isometric efforts, especially at equal relative intensity. For dynamic contractions, the difference is less clear: less fatigue at the elbow in slow contractions, not in fast ones. In a 2024 study cited, women performed more biceps curl repetitions at 50% of their maximum and lost less strength.10 On recovery between sessions, the review reports nothing. I therefore have no data I have read to say that a woman recovers faster or more slowly.

What this means

Fatigability is one of the few areas where women have, on average, an advantage in the studies cited, and it is neither general nor demonstrated for all types of effort. For reading tests: if a test lasts a long time or requires repeated efforts, a smaller gap between the sexes is not surprising. It does not allow any conclusion about your own recovery between two sessions.

Step 6 of 6 · The objections and what remains uncertain

What holds, what does not hold yet, and what comes down to perceptions and habits

Four serious objections arise.

Women’s larger relative gains may come from a lower starting point. The same 3 kg gain is a larger percentage when you start from 10 kg than from 30. This is a natural hypothesis, not tested in the studies read. Roberts and colleagues themselves write that it is possible that untrained women have a greater capacity to increase their upper-body strength, and the 2026 review reminds us that this result should be interpreted with caution, because the studies mix trained and untrained people.4,10

The studies are heterogeneous. The heterogeneity of 72 to 75% for strength in Roberts 2020 means that the studies do not give the same result. Hubal concerns a single muscle and a single type of exercise. Most participants are young and untrained.

The effect of the body cannot be separated from the effect of habits. The comparisons in step 1 are taken at a given moment: they do not know what each person did before. None of the studies read compares men and women with the same training history. The 2026 review only reports that strength training “tends to occupy a higher place among men” and that women more often prefer stretching, yoga or group classes.10 This is a statement without figures. I have not read a quantified participation survey for this article: I therefore cannot say how much of the initial gap comes from a lack of training. What the training studies show is that once people train, progress does not justify a gap in potential.

An average is not a person. The gaps described above are group averages. The range of individual gains (step 4) is almost the same for both sexes. One review also concludes that training should above all be individualised rather than prescribed by sex.10

Questions remain unanswered in what I have read: the role of the menstrual cycle, menopause, hormones, recovery between sessions, or the ideal number of sets for each sex. A study cited by the review suggests that women might respond better to a higher volume of repetitions, with limited evidence.10

The answer to the problem

We had asked the question: what strength gap really exists between men and women, where does it come from, and what does it change for a woman who wants to do strength training?

The gap exists, this is solid. On average, women develop about half to two thirds of men’s strength in absolute terms, with a larger gap for the upper body (Miller’s study, 16 people, confirmed as an order of magnitude by a review). It follows the amount of muscle, this is probable. Strength per muscle area does not differ in the small reference study, and for the legs the gap disappears in athletes after adjusting for lean mass, according to a second-hand review. For the upper body, part of it remains unexplained.

With training, men and women progress comparably in proportion, this is solid for muscle. Hubal (585 people), Roberts (50 studies included) and the 2025 meta-analysis (29 studies) agree on relative muscle gain. For strength, women do as well, or even better in relative terms for the upper body, with a reservation about the starting point. There is no unwanted size gain in these data. The mean gain of a woman following a progressive strength programme is 2.4 cm² of biceps cross-section in 12 weeks, and the differences between people far exceed the difference between the sexes.

What is not established: the share of the starting gap due to habits, recovery between sessions, the effect of the cycle and hormones. The ideas “they progress less” and “they will get huge without wanting to” are not supported. The idea “they are weaker” is true on average and says nothing about an individual.

What to put in place

The following actions follow from this. The retest frequencies are an editorial choice based on the length of the protocols studied (12 weeks in Hubal), not on a study.

  1. Read your norm table for what it is.A norm table separated by sex compares you with people whose average is close to yours: it is the right reference, not a way of setting you a limit. Your level is read against your group, and above all against your own previous result. If the norm table is mixed, remember that the average gap seen in step 1 is enough to explain a lower number without your progress being lower.
  2. Train the upper body like the lower body.The upper body is the area where the starting gap is largest and where women’s relative gains are, according to Roberts, at least as good. That is a reason to work on it more rather than give up on it. Step 3 supports this reading with the reservation from step 6.
  3. Use loads that demand real effort, at least twice a week.The studies read involve progressive programmes of about 12 weeks, with increasing loads. The 2026 review cites a clear health benefit from a practice of at least two sessions per week, but that is a sentence from the review, not a result I re-read at the source.10 Lifting light for fear of getting bulky is not supported by the data read.
  4. Measure on yourself, not on others.Since individual responses range from 0 to 250% for strength, your result is read by comparing your successive attempts. Retest every 8 to 12 weeks, under the same conditions (same time of day, same warm-up, same equipment). A gap smaller than the test’s usual variation does not prove that you are improving.
  5. Do not judge your own potential on an average.If you have progressed little after a block, change the programme and the consistency first before concluding. The data do not allow us to say in advance where you stand between 2 and 59%.

Persistent pain, feeling unwell during exertion or pregnancy justify medical advice before increasing loads.

What these figures do not say
  • Miller’s study covers 16 people. It gives the order of magnitude, not a precise value.1
  • Hubal’s study covers a single muscle, over 12 weeks, in adults aged 18 to 40. One-repetition strength gains in untrained people partly reflect learning the movement.5
  • Several figures (Nuzzo 2023, Bartolomei 2021, Hunter 2014) are reported by a 2026 review and were not re-read at the source.10
  • I did not re-read any study on bone density or any figures from participation surveys for this article: these points are therefore not demonstrated here.
  • Group averages say nothing about an individual.

Frequently asked questions

Will I get bulky if I lift heavy?

In the study of 585 people, a progressive 12-week strength programme gives women on average 2.4 cm² more on the biceps cross-section, with a maximum of 7.2 cm² observed. No study read measures a gain in size “without wanting it”.5

My result is lower than a man’s. Is that bad?

Not in itself. On average, women have less muscle and develop less absolute strength. What matters is your level relative to your norm table and your change from one test to the next.1,2

Should you train differently because you are a woman?

The studies read give no solid reason for a separate prescription. The 2026 review concludes that training should above all be individualised, and cites a study suggesting that women might respond better to more repetitions, with limited evidence.10

Does strength training still work after 50?

Yes, in women as in men: in proportion, strength gains are similar or better for women, and function (chair rises, walking) improves in the same way.8,9
